content: 1. The physiological differences between adolescents and adults are not significant enough to expect a difference in treatment efficacy. This supports the rationale for applying adult treatment evidence to adolescents. 2. Treating adolescents with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), entecavir (ETV), or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is considered safe, with the benefits of treatment outweighing the risks regardless of age, ALT levels, or HBV DNA levels. This is particularly true in cases of fibrosis or cirrhosis, which form the basis for strong treatment recommendations across all age groups, including adults, adolescents, and children. 3. Expanding treatment to adolescents is especially relevant in sub-Saharan Africa, where a significant proportion of the population is under 20 years old, and 25% of those who are HBsAg-positive are younger than 20, compared to 5% or less in other regions. This is partly due to the lack of HBV birth-dose vaccination, which contributes to preventable cases of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) at a young age in this region. 4. In other regions, the prevalence of HBsAg among adolescents and children is low. 5. Expanding treatment criteria may allow for the identification and treatment of adolescents with a strong family history of liver disease, who are at risk of progressing to cirrhosis and HCC in early adulthood. This is particularly important in sub-Saharan Africa, where HCC often occurs at a younger age. 6. Treating adolescent girls of reproductive age may reduce vertical and early horizontal transmission of HBV to infants, which remains the most significant route of transmission globally and accounts for the majority of the global burden of chronic hepatitis B (CHB). 7. Expanding treatment among adolescents with CHB may reduce viral DNA integration events in those with high levels of HBV replication but minimal necroinflammatory changes. Early treatment may prevent severe Tand B-cell dysfunction commonly seen in older individuals. However, direct evidence supporting this is currently lacking. 8. Treatment may improve mental health and reduce self-stigma among adolescents living with hepatitis B by providing reassurance that the risk of transmitting the infection to others is reduced and that the infection is better controlled. 9. Data on the long-term safety of antiviral therapy for adolescents remain limited. For example, one study found that TDF use in children and adolescents was associated with reduced bone density and increased creatinine levels over 72 weeks of treatment. Longer-term studies are needed to determine whether these effects persist and impact peak bone mineral density during adolescence or if they are time-limited, as observed in adults. 10. Long-term TAF treatment in adults with HIV has been associated with weight gain and hyperlipidemia. The extent to which this increases the risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease is not yet clear, and safety data for children using TAF are incomplete. 11. Children and adolescents may experience significant hepatitis flares after discontinuing nucleos(t)ide analogue treatment, sometimes requiring retreatment. This is particularly concerning when treatment is stopped unplanned and without monitoring during adolescence. While this concern should not deter treatment, programs must plan to mitigate risks associated with non-adherence through careful monitoring during treatment. 12. Current evidence is insufficient to support including children younger than 12 years in treatment recommendations for adults and adolescents. Hepatitis B rarely causes significant clinical events in children under 12, and the evidence base for treatment benefits and risks in this age group is even less clear than for adolescents. 13. Treatment for children under 12 is generally offered on a case-by-case basis to those with significant, persistent hepatitis flares, HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, cirrhosis, HCC, or comorbidities that increase the risk of progressive liver disease (e.g., HIV, HCV, or HDV coinfection, iron overload, or the need for immunosuppressive therapy). 14. In a global survey of 150 healthcare workers from 41 countries, respondents prioritized treatment for adolescents with elevated ALT or those who are immunosuppressed. Half of the respondents supported using the same treatment criteria for adolescents as for adults, while 69% believed that treatment criteria for children under 12 should differ from those for adults. 15. Reasons for treating children under 12 differently include the possibility of immune tolerance after neonatal and childhood HBV acquisition, absence of fibrosis or cirrhosis, lower HCC risk, and concerns about long-term treatment safety and dosing recommendations for children. 16. Even in high-income countries, uptake of treatment recommendations for children is low, with only a minority of eligible children and adolescents receiving treatment. Barriers include lack of knowledge, pre-existing beliefs among healthcare practitioners, patients, and families, and limited access to healthcare, diagnostic testing, and medications. 17. Implementing expanded treatment for adolescents requires appropriate resources at every level of care, from diagnosis to treatment initiation and long-term monitoring. Systems must be developed to deliver widespread testing and treatment, especially in high-prevalence areas. 18. Adolescent-friendly services for HIV prevention, testing, and treatment provide an opportunity to integrate similar hepatitis B services. 19. A personand family-centered approach should be adopted, ensuring that uncertainties around benefits, harms, and financial implications of long-term treatment are fully explained. This allows caregivers, adolescents, and healthcare providers to make informed decisions about starting treatment. 20. All countries should incorporate testing for adolescents and children and treatment for adolescents into their national policies and guidelines. This includes focused testing of high-risk populations, such as those with family members with CHB, adolescent boys and men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, and those living with HIV. 21. Simplified treatment eligibility criteria for both adolescents and adults should be easier to implement in lowand middle-income countries, where non-specialist physicians often treat both groups. 22. The age of consent for testing varies across countries and can pose barriers to adolescents' access to services. Adolescent-friendly services and locally sensitive education for healthcare practitioners and target populations are needed to improve HBV testing uptake among adolescents. 23. These guidelines define ALT upper limits of normal (ULN) for children and adolescents as 30 U/L for boys and men and 19 U/L for girls and women, consistent with adult criteria. Other guidelines define adolescent ULN as <22 U/L for girls and <25 U/L for boys. 24. Persistent ALT elevation among adolescents is defined as two ALT values above the ULN within a 6to 12-month period. Treatment trials included only children and adolescents with persistent ALT elevation, as brief, spontaneous ALT elevations are common in this age group and do not show treatment benefits. 25. ALT elevation in this age group may indicate spontaneous HBeAg seroconversion to a sustained state of low viral load and normal ALT, which should be allowed to occur without initiating treatment. 26. Treatment of children depends on the availability of appropriate drug formulations to administer the correct dose. Country programs should review available formulations for procurement, and ongoing efforts aim to make pediatric medicines more widely available. 27. Comparative trials and long-term follow-up studies are needed to determine how treatment during childhood or early adolescence affects liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCC, HBV transmission, and health-related quality of life. 28. Long-term prospective studies are needed to understand the potential adverse effects of long-term nucleos(t)ide analogue treatment on kidney and bone health, including effects on peak bone mass during adolescence and lifetime fracture risk. 29. Long-term follow-up studies should examine the rate of treatment discontinuation and optimal strategies to promote adherence among adolescents and children while minimizing the risks of silent hepatitis flares. 30. Data on the burden and routes of HBV transmission among children and adolescents in different regions and high-risk groups (e.g., adolescents who inject drugs or engage in high-risk sexual behaviors) are needed. 31. Population-based prevalence of liver fibrosis caused by hepatitis B and its progression during childhood should be determined, along with validation of non-invasive tests for liver fibrosis in children and adolescents.
